In cosmological and astrophysical data analysis, a **Delaunay tessellation** is a fundamental geometric framework used to reconstruct continuous, volume-weighted scalar and vector fields from discrete point sets, such as galaxy catalogs or $N$-body simulation particles. Mathematically defined as the dual graph of the Voronoi tessellation, the Delaunay triangulation partitions space into a network of contiguous, non-overlapping simplices (tetrahedra in three dimensions) where the circumsphere of each simplex contains no dataset points in its interior. This unique geometric property provides a self-adaptive foundation for [[density-estimation-techniques|Density estimation techniques]] that naturally scales with local sampling density. By bypassing the arbitrary smoothing scales and symmetric kernels required by standard grid-based mass assignment or [[adaptive-kernel-density-estimation|Adaptive kernel density estimation]], Delaunay-based interpolation seamlessly preserves the extreme density gradients, sharp caustics, and highly anisotropic structural geometries characteristic of the cosmic web [van de Weygaert et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998pcls.work..207V/abstract), [Pelupessy et al. (2003)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2003A&A...403..389P/abstract).

The premier implementation of this spatial framework is the Delaunay Tessellation Field Estimator (DTFE) [Cautun et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ascl.soft05003C/abstract), which serves as the standard methodology for extracting multi-scale kinematic and morphological information from large-scale structure. Beyond density mapping, interpolating across the Delaunay network yields unbiased, volume-averaged estimates of the peculiar velocity field. The resulting velocity divergence distributions are critical for modeling redshift-space distortions and provide a bias-independent constraint on the matter density parameter, $\Omega_m$ [Romano-Díaz et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007MNRAS.382....2R/abstract). Additionally, the underlying simplicial complexes offer a mathematically rigorous basis for higher-order topological analysis. By employing [[alpha-shapes-topology|Alpha Shapes (topology)]] and [[persistent-homology|Persistent homology]], researchers can compute scale-dependent Betti numbers to quantify the complex connectivity of the universe. Furthermore, utilizing [[isodensity-analysis|Isodensity Analysis]] on the tessellation allows for the precise measurement of Minkowski Functionals directly from triangulated surfaces [Aragon-Calvo et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010arXiv1006.4178A/abstract). These morphological tools, originally introduced to cosmology via [[poisson-voronoi-tessellation|Poisson point processes]] [Mecke et al. (1994)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1994A&A...288..697M/abstract), are exquisitely sensitive to the non-Gaussian structural signatures and non-linearities that emerge during late-time gravitational clustering.

Modern applications of Delaunay tessellations continue to expand into diverse astrophysical domains. The framework is now integrated into Bayesian inference models for reconstructing primordial initial conditions, and it serves as an adaptive pixelation grid for source modeling in strong gravitational lensing. Furthermore, software packages like [[disperse|DISPERSE]] utilize the tessellation as the bedrock for robust [[galaxy-filament-finding-algorithm|Galaxy Filament-Finding algorithm]] applications. Despite its widespread adoption, several active research avenues remain, including overcoming the poor recovery rates of small-scale voids in sparse surveys, mapping the extent of "topological bias," and evaluating whether newly developed, biologically-inspired machine learning models might ultimately outperform rigid tessellations in tracing the faintest, most diffuse filaments of the cosmic web.

== Historical Development and Evolution ==
The application of Delaunay and Voronoi tessellations in cosmology originated from attempts to mathematically model the geometric and topological features of the large-scale structure of the Universe. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, the cosmic matter distribution was first conceptualized in terms of a "Voronoi foam" [Icke et al. (1991)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1991QJRAS..32...85I/abstract). In these early cellular models, the Universe was approximated as a packing of polyhedral cells driven by the expansion of underdense voids, with matter sweeping into filamentary and wall-like interstices. The statistical physics approaches of this era even connected these Voronoi patterns to the complex structure of cosmic microwave background (CMB) fluctuations and the Harrison-Zeldovich spectrum [Pietronero et al. (2001)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2002PhyA..306..395P/abstract). A comprehensive review of these cellular models and the Press-Schechter formalism also highlighted their importance in the historical debate over galaxy formation bias [Peacock et al. (1992)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1992LNP...408....1P/abstract).

Even earlier, approaches combining the [[minimal-spanning-tree|Minimal Spanning Tree (MST)]] and Voronoi tessellations provided some of the first objective evidence for filaments in the early Center for Astrophysics (CfA) redshift survey [Ling et al. (1987)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1987PhDT........12L/abstract). Voronoi-based tessellations proved particularly effective during this era; they were successfully used to model the quasi-periodic, sharp density peaks observed in deep "pencil-beam" galaxy redshift surveys [Ikeuchi et al. (1991)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1991MNRAS.250..519I/abstract). Furthermore, they were directly compared against multiplicative multifractals to discriminate between competing clustering paradigms [Martinez et al. (1990)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1990ApJ...357...50M/abstract). This era also saw intense debate regarding the fractal properties and potential homogenization scales of galaxy distributions, underscoring the need for correct methodological estimators to distinguish between true multi-scale fractals and homogeneous distributions at large scales [Sylos Labini et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998astro.ph..1151S/abstract). During this era, researchers also explored cosmology in one dimension, utilizing nearest-neighbor and k-neighbor methods in 1D numerical simulations for computing generalized dimensions in low-density multifractal distributions [Miller et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015arXiv150104674M/abstract). 

Notably, van de Weygaert demonstrated that the spatial two-point correlation function of Voronoi vertices naturally reproduced the power-law behavior and amplitude observed for Abell clusters, suggesting a fundamental connection between cellular geometry and cluster distributions on scales of around $50 \text{ Mpc}$ [van de Weygaert et al. (1989)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1989A&A...213....1V/abstract), while related cellular models and Voronoi foam studies explored this structural behavior across the broader $10$ to $200 \text{ Mpc}$ scale range [Icke et al. (1991)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1991QJRAS..32...85I/abstract). Furthermore, 3D Voronoi methods were specifically adapted to handle the non-homogeneity of the Local Supercluster by overscaling distances based on concentration power laws [Melnyk et al. (2006)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2006KFNT...22..283M/abstract). Additionally, researchers noted that the cellular patterns inherent to the cosmic web may serve as a source of intrinsic "geometrically biased" clustering in the galaxy distribution [van de Weygaert et al. (2007)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007arXiv0707.2877V/abstract). Tessellations also formed the geometric basis for the "adhesion approximation" based on Burgers' equation, which described the Universe as an irregular tiling of space where matter flows sequentially from high-dimensional elements like polyhedral tiles (voids) into lower-dimensional faces, edges (filaments), and finally vertices (clusters) [Shandarin et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009arXiv0912.4520S/abstract). These non-linear geometric models provided a vital complement to early N-body simulations, which were often heavily limited by low dynamic ranges and boundary effects [Icke et al. (1991)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1991QJRAS..32...85I/abstract), [Sahni et al. (1995)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1995PhR...262....1S/abstract).

A significant paradigm shift occurred in the late 1990s when tessellations transitioned from theoretical models of foam-like geometry to practical, data-driven field estimators. Historically, density and velocity fields derived from N-body simulations or discrete galaxy redshift surveys were constructed by interpolating particles onto uniform cubic grids and applying fixed-radius Gaussian smoothing. However, this approach smeared out the highly anisotropic and multiscale structures of the cosmic web. To address this, van de Weygaert and collaborators formalized the use of Delaunay and Voronoi tessellations to reconstruct continuous fields directly from discrete point sets, establishing volume-weighted estimators capable of automatically adjusting to local sampling densities [van de Weygaert et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998pcls.work..207V/abstract). 

With the advent of massive galaxy redshift surveys and the release of highly optimized public software codes [Cautun et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ascl.soft05003C/abstract), Delaunay-based estimators became a foundational tool for mapping the Local Universe. In the modern era, the historical focus on density reconstruction has evolved to include rigorous topological and morphological analyses. This geometric framework allows modern cosmologists to move beyond standard two-point statistics, capturing the signatures of non-linear gravitational evolution and mapping the precise multiscale connectivity of the cosmic web from sparse observational datasets [Lippich et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.508.3771L/abstract), [Liu et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJS..273...33L/abstract).

== Mathematical Foundations and Self-Adaptive Geometry ==
The Delaunay tessellation of a discrete point set—such as observed galaxies or $N$-body simulation particles—partitions space into a set of contiguous, non-overlapping simplicial complexes (tetrahedra in three dimensions). It is mathematically defined as the dual graph of the Voronoi tessellation. The defining geometric property of the Delaunay triangulation is the empty circumsphere criterion: the circumsphere of every constituent simplex contains no points from the dataset in its interior.

This fundamental geometric property allows the tessellation to act as a self-adaptive framework for [[density-estimation-techniques|Density estimation techniques]]. The local density at any vertex is inversely proportional to the volume of its corresponding Voronoi cell or adjacent Delaunay tetrahedra. Unlike traditional Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) or fixed-grid approaches that rely on arbitrary smoothing lengths, the Delaunay-based approach provides an intrinsic form of adaptive smoothing that naturally scales with the local sampling density. By avoiding isotropic smoothing kernels, Delaunay interpolations preserve the local anisotropy and multiscale nature of the cosmic web. They effectively resolve steep density gradients, sharp caustics, and highly flattened or elongated filamentary structures that are typically blurred or artificially broadened by conventional methods [van de Weygaert et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998pcls.work..207V/abstract), [Pelupessy et al. (2003)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2003A&A...403..389P/abstract). Alongside tessellations, structure functions based on the principal moments of inertia within spherical windows were introduced to quantify the relative prevalence of clumps, filaments, and sheets [Babul et al. (1992)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1992ApJ...401...28B/abstract). This simplicial deformation framework also naturally supports the generalization of Eulerian bias models to incorporate Lagrangian descriptions of galaxy motion [Wang et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012PhRvD..86d3508W/abstract).

== The Delaunay Tessellation Field Estimator (DTFE) ==
The Delaunay Tessellation Field Estimator (DTFE) is a highly optimized algorithm designed to reconstruct continuous volume-weighted fields—such as density and velocity—from discrete point sets. Originally developed to overcome the limitations of fixed-scale smoothing in cosmological data [van de Weygaert et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998pcls.work..207V/abstract), DTFE has become a standard methodology for the multi-scale analysis of the cosmic web.

**Field Estimation and Mass Assignment**
Unlike grid-based mass assignment schemes (e.g., Cloud-in-Cell), DTFE utilizes the Delaunay tessellation of a discrete point distribution as a natural, multidimensional interpolation grid [Romano-Díaz et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007MNRAS.382....2R/abstract), [Cautun et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ascl.soft05003C/abstract). The algorithm estimates the local density $\rho_i$ at each sample point $i$ by computing the inverse of the volume of its contiguous Delaunay tetrahedra (the Delaunay macrocell). For a $D$-dimensional space where each point carries a mass $m_i$, the density is inversely proportional to the volume of this contiguous region, $V_i$:

$$ \rho_i \propto \frac{m_i}{V_i} $$

This framework directly motivates the related Voronoi volume function (VVF), a powerful statistical probe of the local number density distribution that is highly sensitive to underlying dark matter models and the large-scale environment [Paranjape et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.495.3233P/abstract). Once the densities at the vertices are established, the field is linearly interpolated across the interior of each Delaunay simplex, ensuring a strictly volume-weighted and continuous reconstruction across the entire domain [Pelupessy et al. (2003)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2003A&A...403..389P/abstract).

**Methodological Tensions and Alternatives**
While DTFE represents a consensus choice for preserving sharp gradients and complex topologies, the literature presents ongoing methodological debate regarding optimal field reconstruction. Comparative studies indicate that higher-order tessellation techniques, such as the Natural Neighbour Field Estimator (NNFE) or Kriging, can produce fields that are smoother and more visually appealing, though DTFE remains vastly superior in computational efficiency [Platen et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.416.2494P/abstract). Furthermore, for specific astronomical datasets, some authors argue that [[adaptive-kernel-density-estimation|Adaptive kernel density estimation]] (such as the Modified Breiman Estimator) offers stronger predictive power and reliability for environmental quantification [Ferdosi et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011A&A...531A.114F/abstract). However, in comparative studies of density field estimation for actual galaxy surveys—such as the analysis of the COSMOS field out to $z \sim 3$—Voronoi tessellation and adaptive kernel smoothing were shown to significantly outperform standard nearest-neighbor methods in accurately tracking galaxy evolution across diverse environments [Darvish et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...805..121D/abstract). Nonetheless, DTFE remains a foundational tool for the topological and kinematic characterization of large-scale structure.

== Kinematics and Velocity Field Statistics ==
The extraction of reliable kinematics and peculiar velocity fields from discrete observational data or $N$-body simulations is notoriously sensitive to sampling geometry. Because Delaunay tetrahedra naturally partition space based on the local tracer density, interpolating velocities across these simplices yields unbiased volume-averaged estimators [van de Weygaert et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998pcls.work..207V/abstract). Furthermore, researchers incorporate the use of spherical harmonic expansions of angular correlations to detect anisotropies in non-random patterns across different scales [Valdarnini et al. (2000)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2001A&A...366..376V/abstract).

A primary application of Delaunay kinematics is the statistical analysis of the local velocity divergence, 
$$ \theta = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} $$
Perturbation theory dictates that the probability distribution function (PDF) and the moments of the velocity divergence exhibit a specific dependence on the cosmic matter density parameter, $\Omega_m$, that is theoretically independent of the linear bias between galaxies and the underlying dark matter [Bernardeau et al. (1996)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997MNRAS.290..566B/abstract). DTFE accurately captures these kinematic signatures, particularly the sharp cutoff in the velocity divergence PDF driven by the maximum expansion rate of cosmic voids. By applying DTFE velocity reconstruction to the PSCz galaxy survey, researchers successfully measured this void expansion cutoff to consistently reproduce a value of $\Omega_m \sim 0.35$ underlying the local velocity dataset [Romano-Díaz et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007MNRAS.382....2R/abstract). Notably, the tessellation method effectively isolates this $\Omega_m$ dependence even when peculiar velocity measurements are restricted to the single component along the line of sight [Bernardeau et al. (1996)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997MNRAS.290..566B/abstract).

Beyond one-point statistics, Delaunay tessellations are vital for computing two-point kinematic clustering, specifically the non-linear velocity divergence auto-power spectrum $P_{\theta\theta}(k)$ and the density-velocity cross-power spectrum $P_{\theta\delta}(k)$. DTFE allows the accurate recovery of these spectra well into the quasi-linear and non-linear regimes, achieving high accuracy on scales of $k < 1 \, h \, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ at redshift $z=0$ [Jennings et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.427L..25J/abstract). Precision modeling of these velocity statistics is essential for characterizing redshift-space distortions (RSDs). Furthermore, because the peculiar velocity field responds more directly to the underlying gravitational potential than the galaxy density field, DTFE-reconstructed velocity spectra serve as a highly sensitive test of gravity, allowing researchers to distinguish between general relativity and modified gravity models [Jennings et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.427L..25J/abstract). Utilizing this sensitivity, researchers also employ Voronoi tessellations to define local density-based "marks" for the marked correlation function; this technique enhances the statistical signature of environment-dependent fifth forces, providing a robust method to discriminate between General Relativity and $f(R)$ gravity models [Armijo et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024MNRAS.529.2866A/abstract).

In the broader context of structure formation, tetrahedral tessellations of the Lagrangian lattice enable the full cosmographic reconstruction of the "dark matter phase-space sheet." This framework measures the deformation of fluid elements, identifies multi-stream regions, and maps large-scale bulk and shear flows directly from observational data [Leclercq et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017JCAP...06..049L/abstract). 

== High-Order Statistics and Minkowski Functionals ==
To characterize the geometry and topology of the cosmic web beyond standard two-point statistics, cosmologists employ morphological measures known as Minkowski Functionals (MFs) [Mecke et al. (1994)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1994A&A...288..697M/abstract). Traditional methods for estimating MFs rely on interpolating discrete galaxy distributions onto a uniform grid and applying a fixed Gaussian smoothing kernel. However, this approach inherently degrades the multiscale structural information of the density field. By contrast, computing MFs directly from the triangulated [[isodensity-analysis|Isodensity Analysis]] of a Delaunay tessellation preserves the exact geometry of the discrete point set without introducing arbitrary smoothing parameters or succumbing to grid-resolution limits [Zhang et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...722..812Z/abstract), [Aragon-Calvo et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010arXiv1006.4178A/abstract). A foundational tutorial provided the computational basis for applying these morphological measures directly to galaxy redshift catalogs [Schmalzing et al. (1996)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1996dmu..conf..281S/abstract). Additionally, conditional subsampling based on MFs allows for the objective extraction of individual building blocks like sheets and filaments from point processes [Platzöder et al. (1995)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1996app..conf..251P/abstract).

In standard cosmological perturbation theory, the initial density field is assumed to be highly Gaussian. Accordingly, all high-order connected moments $\ell > 2$, such as the lowest-order contribution to the third moment $\kappa_3 = \langle \delta^3 \rangle$, are strictly zero, and linear evolution preserves this Gaussianity. However, as structure formation enters the non-linear regime, gravitational clustering induces significant non-Gaussian morphological features. Software implementations such as MEDUSA accurately estimate MFs from 3D Delaunay isodensity surfaces, successfully recovering the non-Gaussian structural signatures that arise exclusively from late-time, non-linear gravitational evolution [Lippich et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.508.3771L/abstract).

Delaunay-based MFs possess robust discriminative power, particularly when confronting observational systematics like redshift-space distortions (RSD) and the Alcock-Paczynski effect. Although RSD alters the measured MFs, expressing these morphological measures as a function of the volume-filling fraction significantly mitigates these distortions [Lippich et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.508.3771L/abstract). Quantitatively, Delaunay-based density field estimation enhances the discriminative power of MFs for RSD effects by approximately two orders of magnitude compared to traditional Gaussian smoothing, and improves the constraining power on the structure growth rate by a factor of $3$ to $5$ [Liu et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJS..273...33L/abstract). However, it is important to acknowledge that large-scale morphology is highly sensitive to cosmic variance on scales much larger than the non-linear length (typically around $8 \text{ Mpc}/h$) [Dominguez et al. (2001)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2001astro.ph..2197D/abstract).

== Topological Analysis and Alpha Shapes ==
The multi-scale connectivity of the cosmic web cannot be fully captured by standard two-point correlation functions. Instead, higher-order topological descriptors are necessary to quantify the complex arrangement of clusters, filaments, walls, and voids [Pranav et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017MNRAS.465.4281P/abstract). For a discrete distribution of galaxies or simulation particles, the topological structure is rigorously defined using [[alpha-shapes-topology|Alpha Shapes (topology)]]. An alpha shape is a simplicial complex constructed as a subset of the Delaunay tessellation, parameterized by a spatial scale $\alpha$. By varying $\alpha$, one generates a filtration—an ordered, nested sequence of sub-complexes that reflects the structural hierarchy of the distance field [van de Weygaert et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011LNCS.6970...60V/abstract), [van de Weygaert et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013arXiv1306.3640V/abstract). 

This filtration provides the computational foundation to evaluate scale-dependent Betti numbers, $\beta_k$, which count the $k$-dimensional topological features of the manifold (e.g., connected components, one-dimensional loops, and two-dimensional enclosed cavities). Betti numbers offer a significantly richer, multiscale description of the cosmic network than the traditional topological genus or Euler characteristic [van de Weygaert et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010arXiv1006.2765V/abstract). Even in simpler forms, such as 2D genus analysis of projected catalogs (like the Lick survey), topology can still reveal non-Gaussian signals despite significant projection effects [Davies et al. (1993)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1993MNRAS.260..553D/abstract). In addition to Betti numbers, percolation analysis based on discrete points (the S-bb relation) provides a robust measure of connectivity that is sensitive to all orders of correlation functions [Zhang et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018PhRvD..97b3534Z/abstract). Historically, the use of percolation and genus curves has been instrumental in differentiating the connectedness of overdense versus underdense regions as they evolve into the non-linear regime [Sahni et al. (1997)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997ApJ...476L...1S/abstract). Complementing these methods, modern network analysis applies structural centralities—such as degree, closeness, and betweenness—and compares these network-derived properties against distinct galaxy populations defined by Voronoi tessellation density, distinguishing central "backbone" structures from surrounding "fracture" regions [Hong et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.450.1999H/abstract).

To distinguish true physical structures from discreteness noise, the Delaunay filtration is heavily analyzed using [[persistent-homology|Persistent homology]]. This mathematical framework tracks the "birth" and "death" of topological features as the scale parameter $\alpha$ increases, effectively isolating the highly significant, persistent skeletal features of the universe from localized statistical fluctuations. These techniques have been validated on a variety of distributions, including Voronoi clustering templates and the fractal-like [[soneira-model|Soneira model]] [Pranav et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017MNRAS.465.4281P/abstract).

The application of Delaunay-based persistent topology has also uncovered novel physical phenomena, most notably **"topological bias."** Persistence and Betti curve analyses have demonstrated a remarkable linear relationship between halo mass and topological environment: dark matter halos of different masses inherently trace structures with distinct topological signatures. This geometric bias operates independently of the standard halo clustering bias derived from two-point statistics, highlighting the necessity of high-order Delaunay methods for precision cosmology [Bermejo et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024MNRAS.529.4325B/abstract). Further investigations using high-volume N-body simulations have shown that halo clustering bias depends on internal concentration up to the fourth order, a result that adds further complexity to the environmental dependence of dark matter halos [Angulo et al. (2007)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008MNRAS.387..921A/abstract).

== Characterizing Voids, Filaments, and Clusters ==
The adaptive nature of Delaunay and Voronoi tessellations makes them exceptionally well-suited for segmenting the cosmic web into its fundamental morphological components.

**Void Identification**
In underdense regions, the Delaunay TrIangulation Void findEr (DIVE) leverages the tessellation to identify empty spherical regions constrained by discrete tracers [Zhao et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016MNRAS.459.2670Z/abstract). While recovering small-scale voids ($< 3 \ h^{-1}\text{Mpc}$) remains highly sensitive to tracer sparsity [Platen et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.416.2494P/abstract), Delaunay-based void statistics offer uniquely sensitive cosmological probes. For instance, massive neutrino free-streaming alters the spatial distribution of halos, which in turn impacts the measured void size distribution: small voids in neutrino-rich regions expand as bounding halos are washed outward, while larger voids are effectively squeezed. This effect significantly skews the Delaunay void number function, providing a potential signature for neutrino mass in galaxy surveys [Qin et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...862...60Q/abstract). In addition to fully 3D finders, researchers have successfully utilized [[poisson-voronoi-tessellation|Poisson Voronoi]] survival functions for modeling the apparent radii and sectional areas of cosmic voids in survey data [Zaninetti et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010SerAJ.181...19Z/abstract). Furthermore, analyses of void scaling have revealed that the rank-ordering of voids in fractal distributions follows Zipf's law, a property that can be effectively used to distinguish "wall" galaxies from isolated "field" galaxies [Gaite et al. (2005)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2005astro.ph.10328G/abstract). Applying Delaunay tessellations to massive datasets like the TianNu simulation demonstrates that tessellation-identified voids act as exceptionally reliable tracers for different density regions, enabling an enhanced detection of the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) signal compared to standard galaxy clustering [Liu et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017arXiv171201002L/abstract).

**Filament Extraction**
For identifying the one-dimensional bridges of the cosmic web, the [[disperse|DISPERSE]] software operates as a robust [[galaxy-filament-finding-algorithm|Galaxy Filament-Finding algorithm]]. It applies discrete Morse theory to Delaunay tessellations to extract the topological skeleton of the density field, filtering out discreteness noise via the concept of persistence [Sousbie et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ascl.soft02015S/abstract). As a new graph-based alternative to DISPERSE, algorithms like T-ReX utilize regularized [[minimal-spanning-tree|minimum spanning trees]] within a Gaussian mixture framework to recover the filamentary pattern [Bonnaire et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020A&A...637A..18B/abstract). Filamentary structure plays a crucial role in environmental galaxy evolution; studies find that over $90\%$ of galaxies reside within $\sim 1.5 \text{ Mpc}$ of a filamentary spine [Hasan et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...970..177H/abstract). In high-density environments, specialized "Galaxy System-Finding" and "Galaxy Filament-Finding" algorithms have been used to detect specific structures, such as 144 filaments mapped in local superclusters, noting that galaxies residing in these filaments show clear evidence of preprocessing and gas accretion [Santiago-Bautista et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020A&A...637A..31S/abstract). 

However, the literature presents a nuanced picture of how filaments affect star formation. Some analyses indicate that low-mass galaxies experience a star formation rate boost (up to $5.9\sigma$) when connected to filamentary streams due to enhanced matter reservoirs [Galárraga-Espinosa et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...671A.160G/abstract). Conversely, other studies emphasize that a high local filament line density efficiently strips gas, leading to the quenching of low-mass galaxies and satellites [Hasan et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...970..177H/abstract). Furthermore, environmental studies show that red galaxy fractions diminish in environments close to voids even at fixed local density, reflecting how large-scale structural modulations override purely local density effects [González et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009MNRAS.397.1498G/abstract).

**Clusters and Global Segmentation**
At the highest densities, inverse Voronoi cell areas and Delaunay-based density peaks are used to locate cluster centroids [Panko et al. (2004)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2004ogci.conf..245P/abstract). Voronoi-based cluster detection is particularly robust for identifying galaxy systems regardless of their morphological shape in imaging surveys [Ramella et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1999ASPC..176..108R/abstract). Following their detection, Bayesian analysis is frequently applied to determine the optimal parameterization of the galaxy cluster mass function extracted from simulation data [Sealfon et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010AN....331..832S/abstract). Combined with caustic analysis, DTFE has successfully identified massive galaxy clusters in the mass range of $10^{12} - 10^{16} M_\odot$, such as the 113 massive clusters mapped in the GAMA survey [Ibarra-Medel et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014arXiv1410.0748I/abstract). To characterize the dynamic environment around these halos, adaptive interpolation of the density field allows for computing the Hessian matrix directly at each halo location. This approach identifies local environmental collapse or expansion more robustly than fixed grids [Wang et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020NewA...8001405W/abstract). Furthermore, morphological classification of superclusters into "spider" and "filament" types has shown how cluster multimodality strongly correlates with these high-density, complex network environments [Einasto et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012A&A...542A..36E/abstract).

== Computational Implementation and Software Tools ==
Applying Delaunay tessellations to massive cosmological datasets poses significant computational challenges. The primary bottleneck is the memory and processing time required to compute a three-dimensional tessellation, which scales non-linearly with the number of tracers. To overcome these barriers, the community has developed highly optimized software packages:

*   **DTFE Code:** The standard tool for continuous field reconstruction is the DTFE public software [Cautun et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ascl.soft05003C/abstract). Written in C++, this code relies on the Computational Geometry Algorithms Library (CGAL) and is accelerated using OpenMP parallelization, outputting volume-weighted density and velocity fields directly from discrete point sets [Cautun et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011arXiv1105.0370C/abstract). 
*   **[[disperse|DISPERSE]] (Discrete Persistent Structures Extractor):** This software applies discrete Morse theory and [[persistent-homology|Persistent homology]] to Delaunay tessellations to identify the multiscale components of the cosmic web. By computing the discrete Morse-Smale complex, DISPERSE extracts statistically robust filamentary spines, walls, and voids directly from noisy distributions [Sousbie et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ascl.soft02015S/abstract).
*   **MEDUSA:** Explicitly designed to measure Minkowski Functionals from large-scale structure data, MEDUSA constructs triangulated surfaces via [[isodensity-analysis|Isodensity Analysis]] of the Delaunay tessellation. Crucially for theoretical cosmology, MEDUSA handles the periodic boundary conditions of synthetic simulation cubes, allowing precision measurements of non-Gaussian signatures in the non-linear density field [Lippich et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.508.3771L/abstract).

== Recent Advances and Future Directions ==
Delaunay tessellation has recently evolved from a foundational tool for density estimation into the geometric backbone for advanced Bayesian reconstruction, high-resolution lensing analysis, and the extraction of higher-order topological statistics. 

**Bayesian Inference and Initial Condition Reconstruction**
Delaunay tessellation mapping is now integral to complex Bayesian inference frameworks designed to reconstruct cosmological initial conditions. The COSMIC BIRTH algorithm [Kitaura et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.502.3456K/abstract) utilizes a tetrahedral tessellation mapping of Lagrangian tracers to efficiently translate light-cone galaxy surveys to a high-redshift initial state, self-consistently accounting for complex survey masks, non-linear bias, and redshift-space distortions.

**Source Reconstruction in Gravitational Lensing**
Beyond large-scale structure, adaptive Delaunay grids are advancing source reconstruction in strong gravitational lensing [Ndiritu et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240719015N/abstract), [Ndiritu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.538..671N/abstract). In multi-band JWST analyses of the cluster lens Abell S1063, pixelated source modeling based on Delaunay triangulation significantly reduced systematic errors compared to standard parametric methods. Parametric approaches were found to produce spurious, high-confidence ($\Delta \text{BIC} > 20$) detections of dark matter subhalos at the $M \sim 10^{10} M_\odot$ mass scale. Delaunay-based source reconstruction strongly alleviates these systematics, proving critical for disentangling genuine dark matter substructure from source-modeling artifacts [Ephremidze et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250218571E/abstract), [Ephremidze et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.542.2610E/abstract). Relatedly, novel scatter-based smoothing methods have been developed to map complex high-order singularities in lensing caustics, such as "swallowtails" and "butterflies," which are critical for interpreting lensing substructures accurately. When directly compared, these advanced scatter methods have been shown to be in good agreement with Delaunay tessellation estimators [Li et al. (2006)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2006ApJ...652...43L/abstract).

**Photometric Redshifts and Broader Applications**
In addition to spatial mapping, Voronoi density estimation is now applied in the multi-dimensional space of photometric parameters to reconstruct the full shape of galaxy redshift distributions and robustly identify outliers in deep surveys [Granett et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017A&C....18...18G/abstract). More broadly, comprehensive reviews of these techniques highlight how Voronoi and Delaunay methods have proliferated across various astronomical subfields, finding applications ranging from constraining cosmic microwave background anomalies to modeling complex fluid dynamics in supernova explosion scenarios [Vavilova et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021inas.book...57V/abstract).

**Topological Bias and Next-Generation Surveys**
Accurately modeling "topological bias" [Bermejo et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024MNRAS.529.4325B/abstract) is crucial for properly interpreting the structural hierarchies mapped by next-generation missions like DESI and the Euclid survey. Delaunay algorithms are already playing a central role in these datasets; for example, the Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1) utilizes the Delaunay-based DETECTIFz algorithm to reliably identify high-redshift ($z > 1.5$) star-forming protoclusters [Euclid Collaboration et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250321304E/abstract).

**Machine Learning and Biologically-Inspired Algorithms**
Despite its broad mathematical success, standard Delaunay methods face emerging challenges from machine learning and biologically-inspired estimators. While DTFE is highly effective for multiscale density reconstruction, recent studies indicate that algorithms such as the Monte Carlo Physarum Machine (MCPM)—inspired by the foraging behavior of slime mold—can outperform DTFE in tracing diffuse, low-prominence cosmic filaments [Hasan et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...970..177H/abstract). When interfaced with topological extractors like [[disperse|DISPERSE]], these bio-inspired models can identify fainter tendrils of the cosmic web that might be fragmented by purely geometric tessellations, pointing toward the development of hybrid [[density-estimation-techniques|Density estimation techniques]] in the future.
